The Java Collections Framework provides a rich suite of thread-safe data structures under the java.util.concurrent package, moving away from legacy synchronized wrappers like Collections.synchronizedMap. These concurrent collections are architected to maximize throughput under high contention by leveraging fine-grained locking, lock-free algorithms, and atomic memory operations. Rather than locking the entire underlying structure during an operation, modern concurrent collections utilize Compare-And-Swap (CAS) primitives and sophisticated node-based memory layouts to allow simultaneous reads and writes without thread interference, preventing the catastrophic throughput bottlenecks seen in synchronized monitors.

At the heart of this architecture are specialized implementations like ConcurrentSkipListMap and ConcurrentLinkedQueue. ConcurrentSkipListMap serves as a concurrent, lock-free equivalent to a sorted map, maintaining keys in ascending natural order or via a custom Comparator while supporting safe concurrent navigation and updates. It implements a concurrent skip list—a probabilistic data structure composed of parallel linked lists with multiple levels of forward pointers that allow logarithmic search times. On the other hand, ConcurrentLinkedQueue is an unbounded, thread-safe, lock-free queue based on the classic Michael-Scott algorithm. It relies heavily on volatile pointer writes and atomic CAS loops on head and tail nodes to achieve extreme throughput for producer-consumer workloads without blocking threads.

items: ConcurrentSkipListMap avoids locking by using randomized tower heights for nodes, where higher-level index pointers are spliced into the list atomically via CAS loops, ensuring that traversals can bypass large sections of data lock-free.

ConcurrentLinkedQueue employs a weakly consistent iterator, meaning it reflects elements as of some point at or since the creation of the iterator, never throwing ConcurrentModificationException and operating safely alongside concurrent mutations.

Lock-free algorithms in java.util.concurrent depend heavily on Java Memory Model (JMM) volatile semantics, ensuring that modifications made to node references and item payloads are immediately visible to other threads via happens-before relationships established by volatile reads and writes.

parsed_answer.content: Beware of structural size operations! Methods like size() and isEmpty() on concurrent collections such as ConcurrentSkipListMap and ConcurrentLinkedQueue are not O(1) operations. Because there is no global lock, computing the exact size requires traversing the entire structure, which can degrade performance significantly in production environments under high throughput. Always avoid calling size() inside performance-critical tight loops.
